title: Does a weather-dependent heat-pump COP change the sand-store versus heat-pump verdict?
summary: The earlier cost comparisons charge the air-source heat pump a flat November–March price divided by one table COP of 3.6. Here the pump's electricity cost is the heat-weighted mean of price / COP(T) over every hour, with hourly temperatures from the ERA5 reanalysis (five German cities, population-weighted, 2015–2019) and the Staffell et al. (2012) COP fit used by when2heat and PyPSA-Eur. The table's 3.6 is what a 35 °C floor-heating sink gives (seasonal COP 3.52–3.67); a 45 °C sink gives 2.79–2.91 and a 55 °C radiator sink 2.18–2.28. The store's weekly-cycling flip multiplier rises from 1.16/1.20/1.20/0.59/1.02 (table) to 1.25/1.29/1.33/0.71/1.15 at 45 °C and 1.37/1.40/1.48/0.86/1.30 at 55 °C, so a realistic COP widens the store's margin in four years but 2018 still favours the pump. Daily cycling stays robust (flip 2.4–4.1×). The heating base temperature (12–18 °C) moves the flip by at most 0.06. Inputs not from a source: the 15 °C base, city weights and the sink temperatures, which are swept; the COP fit is a published regression, not a measurement of a specific unit.
lede: does a weather-dependent heat-pump COP change the sand-store verdict? The table's 3.6 equals a 35 C floor-heating sink; at 45 to 55 C the store's weekly flip multiplier rises 8 to 46%, and 2018 still favours the pump.
